slides.title: Why Study Probability in Business?
slides.text:
Why Study Probability in Business?
Decisions under uncertainty are everywhere in management!
Examples:
Will a new product launch succeed?
What’s the likelihood a key client defaults on payment?
How do supply chain disruptions affect fulfillment rates?

slides.title: What is Probability?
slides.text:
What is Probability?
Probability quantifies uncertainty by assigning a number from 0 to 1 for the likelihood that an event occurs.
In business:
Probability helps gauge risk, optimise resources, and improve forecasting.

bullets.text: Probability quantifies uncertainty by assigning a number from 0 to 1 for the likelihood that an event occurs.

slides.title: Types of Probability
slides.text:
Types of Probability
Classical (Theoretical): All outcomes equally likely (e.g., dice, coins).
Empirical (Relative Frequency): Based on observations or experiments (e.g., late deliveries out of the last 100).
Subjective: Based on personal judgment/experience (e.g., a manager’s estimate).

bullets.text: Classical (Theoretical): All outcomes equally likely (e.g., dice, coins).
Empirical (Relative Frequency): Based on observations or experiments (e.g., late deliveries out of the last 100).
Subjective: Based on personal judgment/experience (e.g., a manager’s estimate).

slides.title: Key Probability Terminology
slides.text:
Key Probability Terminology
Experiment: Any repeatable process with uncertain outcome (e.g., rolling dice, shipping a product).
Outcome: The result of a single trial (e.g., “product arrives late”).
Sample Space (S): The set of all possible outcomes.
Event: A subset of outcomes (e.g., “shipment is delivered” or “at least one defective item”)

slides.title: Example 1
slides.text:
Example 1
An ace is drawn from a deck of cards. The sample space is 52 cards. All the cards have an equal probability of getting accepted.
What is the probability of getting an Ace when picking one card from a deck of 52 cards?
What is the probability of picking up an Ace of Hearts?
Answer:
a) 4/52=1/13 Since a deck has 4 aces and 52 cards, the size of A is 4 and the size of the sample space is 52. Therefore, the probability of A is equal to 4/52.
b)1/52. Ace of Hearts is 1, and the total number of cards is 52

slides.title: Business Example – Probability in Action
slides.text:
Business Example – Probability in Action
Case 1: A logistics manager notices that, on average, 4 out of 100 deliveries are late. What’s the probability that a random delivery will be late next week?
A: 4/100 = 0.04 or 4%
Case 2: A loan officer knows that, historically, 3 out of every 100 business loan applications result in default. What’s the probability a new applicant will default on their loan?
A: 3/100 = 0.03, or 3%
Case 3: A retail manager observes that, during the past 200 sales days, 10 days resulted in key item stockouts. What’s the probability of a stockout on any given sales day?
A: 10/200 = 0.05, or 5%

slides.title: Probability Rules
slides.text:
Probability Rules
Rule 1: 0 ≤ P(Event) ≤ 1
Rule 2: P(Certain event) = 1 (e.g., order is either delivered or not)
Rule 3: P(Complement) = 1 – P(Event)
Probability order NOT being late = 1 – 0.04 = 0.96
Addition Rule (for “or” events):
If mutually exclusive, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B)
Multiplication Rule (for “and” events):
If independent, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)

slides.title: Mutually Exclusive, Independent and Exhaustive Events
slides.text:
Mutually Exclusive, Independent and Exhaustive Events
Mutually Exclusive: Two events can’t happen at the same time (e.g., shipment arrives late and on time).
P(A and B)=0
Independent: The occurrence of one doesn’t affect the other (e.g., two unrelated shipments).
P(A and B)=P(A)×P(B)
Mutually Exhaustive: A set of events is mutually exhaustive if at least one of the events must occur, covering all possible outcomes. (For a single die roll, the events "1", "2", "3", "4", "5", and "6" are mutually exhaustive because the roll must show one of these numbers.)
P(A1 or A2 or … or An) = 1

slides.title: Conditional Probability in Business
slides.text:
Conditional Probability in Business
Definition: The probability of an event, given that another has occurred.
Formula: P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B)
Example: Probability a customer buys a warranty, given they purchased a premium product

Example
Of the population of age 16-21 in a locality, 13.5% are unemployed. 29.5% are high school dropouts, and 5.32% are unemployed high school dropouts. What is the probability that a person in that age group is unemployed, given that he is a high school dropout?
U = the event of being unemployed
D = the event of high school dropouts

slides.title: Practice Problem 2
slides.text:
Practice Problem 2
A machine produces components for use in cellular phones. At any given time, the machine may be in one, and only one, of three states: operational, out of control, or down. From experience with this machine, a quality control engineer knows that the probability that the machine is out of control at any moment is 0.02, and the probability that it is down is 0.015.
What is the relationship between the two events “machine is out of control” and “machine is down”?
When the machine is either out of control or down, a repair person must be called. What is the probability that a repair person must be called right now?
Unless the machine is down, it can be used to produce a single item. What is the probability that the machine can be used to produce a single component right now? What is the relationship between this event and the event “machine is down”?
Answer: a) mutually exclusive
b) 0.035
c) 0.985, complement event

slides.title: Practice Problem 3
slides.text:
Practice Problem 3
As part of a drive to modernize the economy, the government of an eastern European country is pushing for starting 100 new projects in computer development and telecommunications. Two U.S. giants, IBM and AT&T, have signed contracts for these projects: 40 projects for IBM and 60 for AT&T. Of the IBM projects, 30 are in the computer area and 10 are in telecommunications; of the AT&T projects, 40 are in telecommunications and 20 are in computer areas. Given that a randomly chosen project is in telecommunications, what is the probability that it is undertaken by IBM?
Hint: If we see this directly from the fact that there are 50 telecommunications projects and 10 of them are by IBM. This confirms the definition of conditional probability in an intuitive sense.
Answer: 0.2

Practice Problem 4
A consulting firm is bidding for two jobs, one with each of two large multinational corporations. The company executives estimate that the probability of obtaining the consulting job with firm A, event A, is 0.45. The executives also feel that if the company gets the job with firm A, then there is a 0.90 probability that firm B will also give the company the consulting job. What are the company's chances of getting both jobs?
Answer: 0.405

slides.title: Practice Problem 5
slides.text:
Practice Problem 5
Twenty-one per cent of the executives in a large advertising firm are at the top salary level. It is further known that 40% of all the executives at the firm are women. Also, 6.4% of all executives are women and are at the top salary level. Recently, a question arose among executives at the firm as to whether there is any evidence of salary inequity. Assuming that some statistical considerations are met, do the percentages reported above provide any evidence of salary inequity?
Answer: 6.4% < 8.4% Women are underrepresented at the top salary level relative to their overall presence at the firm, as only 6.4% of executives are women at the top, while it would be 8.4% if there were no systemic discrepancy.

slides.title: Discrete Random Variables
slides.text:
Discrete Random Variables
A random variable is a variable that assumes numerical values that are determined by the outcome of an experiment.
Random variable has a probability distribution. We usually denote the random variable by a capital letter, often X. The probability distribution will then be denoted by P(X ).
Suppose there is a scenario that involves the possible options for the birth of 4 babies.

slides.title: Discrete and Continuous Random Variables
slides.text: Discrete and Continuous Random Variables
slides.visual_text: Discrete random variable: can assume at most a countable number of values. For example, the amount of money you make on an investment may be $500, or it may be a loss: -$200; it can be measured at best to the nearest cent, so this variable is discrete. Continuous random variable: may take on any value in an interval of numbers (its possible values are uncountably infinite); its values can be measured (at least in theory) to any degree of accuracy, e.g. temperature (36.111000099 degrees), weight, height, time. Box: the probability distribution of a discrete random variable X must satisfy two conditions: 1. P(x) >= 0 for all values x; 2. the sum of P(x) over all x = 1. Picture: Discrete shown as a stack of money, three cars and six cubes; Continuous shown as a weighing scale, a clock, a thermometer and a ruler. Bottom box: All values of x represents mutually exclusive events and thereby overall probability of all events when summed together will be 1.

slides.title: Cumulative Probability Distribution Function (CDF)
slides.text:
Cumulative Probability Distribution Function (CDF)
The probability distribution of a discrete random variable lists the probabilities of occurrence of different values of the random variable.
Cumulative Probability - Probability that the value of the random variable is at most some value x. This is the sum of all the probabilities of the values I of X that are less than or equal to x.

bullets.text: The probability distribution of a discrete random variable lists the probabilities of occurrence of different values of the random variable.
Cumulative Probability - Probability that the value of the random variable is at most some value x. This is the sum of all the probabilities of the values I of X that are less than or equal to x.

slides.visual_text: A boxed definition: The cumulative distribution function, F(x), of a discrete random variable X is F(x) = P(X <= x) = the sum of P(i) over all i <= x.

slides.title: Example
slides.text: Example
slides.visual_text: Same two-dice text as the previous example, plus: Q2. What is the probability that sum of numbers on two dice will be at most 5? P(X <= 5). Q3. What is the probability that sum of numbers on two dice will be greater than & equal to 9? P(X >= 9). The same dice grid picture. Worked answers: P(X<=5) = P(2) + P(3) + P(4) + P(5) = 1/36 + 2/36 + 3/36 + 4/36 = 10/36. P(X > 9) = P(10) + P(11) + P(12) = 3/36 + 2/36 + 1/36 = 6/36 = 1/6. A callout with arrows to both: These are also known as Cumulative Probability Distributions.

Expected Values of Discrete Random Variables
EV: Measure of centrality of the distribution. The mean of the probability distribution of a random variable is called the expected value of the random variable (sometimes called the expectation of the random variable).

bullets.text: EV: Measure of centrality of the distribution. The mean of the probability distribution of a random variable is called the expected value of the random variable (sometimes called the expectation of the random variable).

slides.visual_text: A boxed definition: The expected value of a discrete random variable X is equal to the sum of all values of the random variable, each value multiplied by its probability: mu = E(X) = the sum over all x of x P(x) (labelled equation 3-4).

slides.title: Variance and Standard Dev of a Random Variable
slides.text:
Variance and Standard Dev of a Random Variable
Variance is a measure of the dispersion of the possible values of the random variable about the mean. The variance gives us an idea of the variation or uncertainty associated with the random variable.
Since the variance is a squared quantity, it is often more useful to consider its square root—the standard deviation of the random variable. When two random variables are compared, the one with the larger variance (standard deviation) is the more variable one.
When comparing two investments with the same average (expected ) return, the investment with the higher standard deviation is considered riskier (although a higher standard deviation implies that returns are expected to be more variable—both below and above the mean).
Probabilities of the values of the random variable are used as weights in the computation of the expected squared deviation from the mean of a discrete random variable

slides.title: Variance and Standard Dev of a Random Variable
slides.text: Variance and Standard Dev of a Random Variable
slides.visual_text: Three boxed formulas. Method 1: The variance of a discrete random variable X is given by sigma squared = V(X) = E[(X - mu) squared] = the sum over all x of (x - mu) squared P(x). Method 2: Computational formula for the variance of a random variable: sigma squared = V(X) = E(X squared) - [E(X)] squared. The standard deviation of a random variable: sigma = SD(X) = the square root of V(X).

slides.title: Example 2: Solution
slides.text: Example 2: Solution
slides.visual_text: Heading line: Refer to Example 7, The profit is given by 2X - 8,000. Box 1: E(X squared) = (5,000) squared (0.2) + (6,000) squared (0.3) + (7,000) squared (0.2) + (8,000) squared (0.2) + (9,000) squared (0.1) = 46,500,000. Text: The expected value of X is E(X) = 6,700. The variance of X is thus: Box 2: V(X) = E(X squared) - [E(X)] squared = 46,500,000 - (6,700) squared = 1,610,000. Text: Finally, we find the variance of the profit, using equation 3-10, as 2 squared (1,610,000) = 6,440,000. The standard deviation of the profit is the square root of 6,440,000 = 2,537.72.

slides.title: Bernoulli Distribution
slides.text:
Bernoulli Distribution
The experiment consists of n identical trials.
Each trial results in a success or a failure.
The probability of a success on any trial is p and remains constant from trial to trial. This implies that the probability of failure, q , on any trial is and remains constant from trial to trial.
The trials are independent (that is, the results of the trials have nothing to do with each other)

slides.title: Bernoulli Distribution
slides.text:
Bernoulli Distribution
If the outcome of a trial can only be either a success or a failure, then the trial is a Bernoulli trial.
The number of successes X in one Bernoulli trial, which can be 1 or 0, is a Bernoulli random variable.
E.g.: While tossing a coin, if we take heads as 1 (success) and tails as 0 (failure), then the outcome of a toss is a Bernoulli random variable.

The probability of the event’s occurrence is the same for any two intervals of equal length, and

Then, the probability that the event will occur x times in a specified interval is

slides.title: Continuous Probability Distribution
slides.text:
Continuous Probability Distribution
A continuous random variable can assume any value in an interval on the real line or in a collection of intervals.
It is not possible to talk about the probability of the random variable assuming a particular value.
Instead, we talk about the probability of the random variable assuming a value within a given interval.
The probability of the random variable assuming a value within some given interval from x1 to x2 is defined to be the area under the graph of the probability density function between x1 and x2

slides.title: Normal Distribution
slides.text:
Normal Distribution
The normal probability distribution is the most important distribution for describing a continuous random variable.
It is widely used in statistical inference. (also known as the Gaussian distribution)
It has been used in a wide variety of applications:
Heights of people
Scientific measurements
Test scores
Amounts of rainfall

slides.title: Characteristics of Normal Distribution
slides.text:
Characteristics of Normal Distribution
The distribution is symmetric; its skewness measure is zero.
The entire family of normal probability distributions is defined by its mean μ and its standard deviation σ
The highest point on the normal curve is at the mean, which is also the median and mode
The mean can be any numerical value: negative, zero, or positive.
The standard deviation determines the width of the curve: larger values result in wider, flatter curves.
Probabilities for the normal random variable are given by areas under the curve. The total area under the curve is 1 (0.5 to the left of the mean and 0.5 to the right).

Standard Normal Distribution
A random variable having a normal distribution with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1 is said to have a standard normal probability distribution.
The letter z is used to designate the standard normal random variable.
Converting to the Standard Normal Distribution
We can think of z as a measure of the number of standard deviations x is from μ.

slides.title: Central Limit Theorem
slides.text:
Central Limit Theorem
The Central Limit Theorem states that, for any population with a finite mean and variance, the sampling distribution of the mean approaches a normal distribution as the sample size increases, regardless of the shape of the population distribution. This means:
For large sample sizes (usually n ≥ 30), the means of repeated samples will be approximately normally distributed.
The mean of these sample means equals the population mean.
The variability (standard deviation) decreases with increasing sample size, as the sample means cluster more tightly around the true population mean.

slides.title: Central Limit Theorem: Practical Relevance
slides.text:
Central Limit Theorem: Practical Relevance
The CLT allows the use of normal probability theory even when the original data is not normal.
Enables calculation of confidence intervals and hypothesis testing about population parameters based on sample data, even for non-normal populations.
Used in fields such as election polling, quality control, finance, and estimating average outcomes in populations.
